reviews.author: Brent Marchant
reviews.content: Stories about challenged individuals who manage to turn their lives around are immensely popular with moviegoing audiences. But there’s a big difference between those that depict individuals who beat the odds against them and those featuring characters who have to dig themselves out of their own self-created holes (and it should be easy to guess which ones are more well-liked). Such latter circumstances are the ones in play in this biographical comedy-drama from writer-director Matt Johnson, an origin story about how celebrity chef and culinary travelogue host Anthony Bourdain (1956-2018) got his start. In 1975, Bourdain (who curtly and routinely informed others that he simply wanted to be called “Tony”) (Dominic Sessa) was enrolled at Vassar College in one of the first classes to which men had been admitted to the former all-women’s institution. He was seeking (with brazenly conceited confidence and no credible experience) a writing fellowship that would allow him avoid going home for the summer, a prospect he viewed with palpable disdain. However, when he was turned down for the opportunity, he needed to find a different path. He decided to head to the coastal resort town of Provincetown, MA to pursue his romantic interest (or, more accurately, romantic obsession) from high school, currently a Vassar co-ed, Nancy Putkoski (Emilia Jones), who was spending the summer on Cape Cod. Tony told others that he was making the journey to work on the fellowship he didn’t win as a cover for his pursuit of a relationship with someone who typically responded to his advances with ambivalence. These conditions ostensibly forced him to wing it in every conceivable way upon arrival in P-town. And, as fate would have it, the “aspiring writer” was the same loutish narcissist there that he was beforehand. After a series of questionable misadventures, he sheepishly ended up taking a job as a dishwasher in a restaurant run by a demanding taskmaster chef (Antonio Banderas) staffed by an array of colorful co-workers (Leo Woodall, Stavros Halkias) who were anything but positive influences. But, as Tony’s summer unfolded, he unwittingly began turning things around, largely thanks to the chef’s stringent tutelage, launching Tony down another new path that would lead him to a storied future. Bourdain’s subsequent success is not depicted here except in the film’s electronic epilogue, but it’s that implication that arguably grants this story its salvation in light of how it starts out. The protagonist is clearly depicted as an admittedly charismatic (though undeniably uncouth) bad boy who probably wouldn’t have otherwise been cut any slack were it not for his accomplishments later in life. Fittingly, Sessa capably makes the most of that characterization, turning in a badass portrayal and a remarkably on-point impersonation of the title character, even if it’s written rather monodimensionally and delivered through an uncannily familiar performance to the actor’s role in “The Holdovers” (2023) (which, unavoidably, raises potential questions about typecasting). It also doesn’t help that Tony’s back story is largely missing, with virtually no explanation behind his motivations, behavior and attitude at this time of his life other than through an epigraphic quote from Bourdain at the film’s outset. And this oversight, for what it’s worth, may leave viewers wondering why they should care about what happens to him. Those considerations aside, though, the picture has definite strengths of note, particularly the impressive supporting cast of Banderas, Woodall and Halkias, who do much to bolster viewer interest in the narrative. The film’s superb period piece production design and fine cinematography also add much to the picture, particularly the character of this release’s time frame. Overall, though, “Tony” feels as though it could have been stronger, better focused and more engaging. It’s modestly entertaining, but, in coming away from it, I felt as though I was only served appetizers and missed out on the main course.

aiEnrichment.summary_one_sentence: In the summer of his youth, a 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain arrives in Provincetown and discovers a passion for culinary chaos while working in a hectic restaurant kitchen.
aiEnrichment.summary_short: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain ventures to the seaside town of Provincetown looking for work and direction. Upon landing a job in a fast-paced restaurant kitchen, he is immediately immersed in a high-intensity world of culinary madness and colorful characters. The experiences, challenges, and camaraderie he encounters over that formative summer fundamentally alter his outlook. Ultimately, this chaotic season sets off the trajectory that will define the rest of his life.
aiEnrichment.summary_long: At nineteen years old, Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown, Massachusetts, seeking purpose and adventure during a crucial crossroads in his youth. Expecting a simple seasonal getaway, his trajectory dramatically shifts when he stumbles into the bustling, high-stakes environment of a local restaurant kitchen. Surrounded by an eclectic crew of passionate chefs, eccentric line cooks, and demanding patrons, he is thrown directly into the fire of line cooking. The intense heat, unrelenting pressure, and sheer chaos of commercial cooking prove to be both overwhelming and deeply exhilarating. Through trial, error, and late-night exhaustion, Bourdain begins to find his rhythm behind the line and earn the respect of his crewmates. The high-stress environment serves as an unconventional classroom, instilling in him a deep discipline, respect for food, and a lifelong devotion to restaurant culture. Beyond the kitchen, the freedom and subculture of Provincetown during the summer months shape his developing identity and worldview. As the season comes to a close, Bourdain realizes that his initial summer job has transformed into something much greater. The indelible bonds forged in the kitchen ultimately spark the passion that shapes the rest of his legendary career.
aiEnrichment.synopsis: Set in the vibrant seaside destination of Provincetown, this drama follows a 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain during a pivotal summer that transformed his life. Finding himself immersed in the chaotic, high-pressure world of a professional restaurant kitchen, Bourdain is exposed to the intense camaraderie, culinary rigor, and raw energy of food preparation. As he navigates the wild summer heat and demanding kitchen culture, he discovers a newfound calling that sets the stage for his future.

story_structure.climax: During the peak of the busy season, the kitchen faces an overwhelming service crisis that tests Anthony's stamina, skill, and commitment to the trade.
story_structure.conflict: Anthony must adapt to the high-pressure, chaotic culture of the professional kitchen while balancing his personal identity and artistic ambitions.
story_structure.resolution: Anthony reflects on his transformational summer in Provincetown, having discovered a lifelong passion for culinary work and defined his future path.
story_structure.introduction: 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain arrives in Provincetown during the summer, looking for direction and taking an entry-level position at a local restaurant.
story_structure.risingAction: As the summer rush intensifies, Anthony earns the respect of his co-workers, gets promoted to higher-stakes kitchen stations, and embraces the intense lifestyle of culinary line work.
